[[File:Stoneley wave.gif|thumb|The motion of the Stoneley wave.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www-odp.tamu.edu/publications/205_SR/206/206_f3.htm | title=Figure F3. Stoneley wave motion (figure after Qobi et al., 2001)}}</ref>]]

A '''Stoneley wave''' is a boundary wave (or interface wave) that typically propagates along a solid-solid interface.<ref>{{cite book |title= Encyclopedic Dictionary of Applied Geophysics|last= Sheriff|first= Robert E.|year=2002 |publisher= Society of Exploration Geophysicists|isbn= 978-1-56080-118-4}}</ref> When found at a liquid-solid interface, this wave is also referred to as a [[Scholte wave]].<ref>{{Cite journal | url=http://downloads.hindawi.com/journals/jam/2012/313207.pdf | title=Rayleigh's, Stoneley's, and Scholte's Interface Waves in Elastic Models Using a Boundary Element Method | author1=Esteban Flores-Mendez| author2=Manuel Carbajal-Romero| author3=Norberto Flores-Guzmán| author4= Ricardo Sánchez-Martínez | author5=Alejandro Rodríguez-Castellanos| journal=Journal of Applied Mathematics | date=2012 | volume=2012 | issue=1 | doi=10.1155/2012/313207 | doi-access=free }}</ref> The wave is of maximum intensity at the interface and decreases exponentially away from it. It is named after the British seismologist Dr. Robert Stoneley (1894–1976), a lecturer in the [[University of Leeds]], who discovered it on October 1, 1924.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Stoneley | first = R. | title = Elastic waves at the surface of separation of two solids | journal = Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A | volume = 106 | issue = 738 | pages = 416–428 | date = October 1, 1924 | doi = 10.1098/rspa.1924.0079|bibcode = 1924RSPSA.106..416S | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Occurrence and use==
Stoneley waves are most commonly generated during borehole [[sonic logging]] and [[Vertical seismic profile|vertical seismic profiling]]. They propagate along the walls of a fluid-filled [[borehole]]. They make up a large part of the low-frequency component of the signal from the seismic source and their attenuation is sensitive to fractures and formation [[permeability (earth sciences)|permeability]]. Recent studies have found that Stoneley wave processing in borehole help to distinguish between fractured versus non-fractured coal seam.<ref>Banerjee, A & Chatterjee, R (2021), Fracture analysis using Stoneley wave in a coalbed methane reservoir. Near Surface Geophysics, https://doi.org/10.1002/nsg.12176</ref> Therefore, analysis of Stoneley waves can make it possible to estimate these rock properties. The standard data processing of sonic logs to derive wave velocity and [[energy]] content is explained in<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.slb.com/~/media/Files/resources/oilfield_review/ors06/spr06/03_borehole_acoustic_waves.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304045842/http://www.slb.com/~/media/Files/resources/oilfield_review/ors06/spr06/03_borehole_acoustic_waves.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-04 | title=Schlumberger Oilfield Glossary – Borehole Acoustic Waves }}</ref> and.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www-odp.tamu.edu/publications/205_SR/206/206_2.htm | title=Introduction}}</ref>

==Comparison to other waves==
A number of wave modes have been predicted based on the fluidity of the medium.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ndt-ed.org/EducationResources/CommunityCollege/Ultrasonics/Physics/modepropagation.htm |title=Modes of Sound Wave Propagation |access-date=2012-05-02 |archive-date=2014-02-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140216095903/http://www.ndt-ed.org/EducationResources/CommunityCollege/Ultrasonics/Physics/modepropagation.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Kubotera, A.|year=1957|title=Rayleigh and Sezawa waves generated by explosions|url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpe1952/5/1/5_1_33/_pdf|journal=Journal of Physics of the Earth|volume=5|issue=1|pages=33–41|doi=10.4294/jpe1952.5.33|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Effects of permeability ==
[[Permeability (earth sciences)|Permeability]] can influence Stoneley wave propagation in three ways. Stoneley waves can be partly reflected at sharp impedance contrasts such as fractures, lithology, or borehole diameter changes. Moreover, as formation permeability increases, Stoneley wave [[velocity]] decreases, thereby inducing dispersion. The third effect is the attenuation of Stoneley waves.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www-odp.tamu.edu/publications/205_SR/206/206_4.htm | title=Method: {{as written|Aqui|stion [sic]}} and Processing of Acoustic Waves in Boreholes}}</ref>
